extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties in inter partes review (IPR) proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, IPR counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether to institute inter partes review of a patent by (1) construing relevant claim terms only as necessary, (2) assessing written‑description support (including for negative limitations), and (3) determining whether the petition shows a reasonable likelihood of proving unpatentability (obviousness) over the cited prior art, with attention to §325(d) discretionary denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description support for negative limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A negative limitation need not be recited in the specification verbatim, but 'there generally must be something in the specification that conveys to a skilled artisan that the inventor intended the exclusion, such as a discussion of disadvantages or alternatives.' (Novartis Pharms. Corp. v. Accord Healthcare, Inc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To support importing a negative limitation into a claim, the specification must convey to a POSITA that the exclusion was intended. Look for express statements, discussions of disadvantages/alternatives, or other disclosure indicating intent to exclude. Mere silence is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from preferred embodiments (Liebel‑Flarsheim)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally improper to read limitations from a preferred embodiment into a claim (the Liebel‑Flarsheim principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the specification discloses an embodiment that includes a particular feature, you should not automatically limit claim scope to that embodiment. Written‑description support for a feature (including a negative limitation) is necessary to import it, but is not sufficient if doing so would improperly read a preferred embodiment limitation into the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit claim construction to terms in controversy and only as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts/Boards 'need only construe terms that are in controversy, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy.' (Nidec Motor Corp. v. Zhongshan Broad Ocean Motor Co., quoting Vivid Techs.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only construe claim terms when necessary for resolving the institution question or the specific dispute; avoid broader or unnecessary constructions. Parties may later brief constructions at trial if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard — reasonable likelihood of prevailing on unpatentability under §103(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of instituting IPR, the Petition must demonstrate a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner will prevail in establishing that the challenged claims are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. §103(a) over the cited prior art (e.g., a asserted combination of references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preliminary record must show that the combination of references and arguments sufficiently addresses each claim limitation and provides a reasonable likelihood of proving obviousness. The Board evaluates the petition's factual and claim‑by‑claim showings at the institution stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness combination test — motivation to combine and predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is obvious if a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine prior art teachings and would have expected to obtain predictable results (e.g., applying a known technique to a known device to yield predictable results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting obviousness over a combination (here, Wu + Doherty), show (a) how each limitation is taught or suggested, (b) a reason a POSITA would combine the references (benefits, commonplace approach), and (c) that the combination yields predictable results. Isolated teachings should not be considered without a rationale to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description support is necessary but not sufficient to import limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Written‑description support for a limitation (including negative limitations) is a necessary condition to import that limitation into a claim, but is not sufficient by itself to justify importing a limitation from the specification into a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the specification contains language that could support a limitation, courts/boards must still avoid importing limitations improperly (see Liebel‑Flarsheim). The party seeking to import a limitation must show both support and that importing is proper in light of claim language and the specification as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not limit claims to a single example or embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally improper to limit claim scope based on a single example; claims should not be confined to one disclosed embodiment absent clear disavowal or lexicographic intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about relying on one embodiment to define claim scope. The Board will not construe claims to the scope of a single example unless the specification clearly requires it; parties should present broader claim meaning only when necessary and supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary claim interpretation may incorporate disclosed examples for institution
rubrics_metrics.description: For institution purposes, certain claim interpretations may reasonably include disclosed examples when the specification and record support that reading (e.g., 'changing a predetermined advertisement insertion point ...' includes skipping over an insertion point to arrive at a different insertion point in response to user activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At institution, the Board may adopt a preliminary interpretation informed by the specification's examples and operation. Parties will have opportunity to brief construction and factual issues later at trial; the institution interpretation is limited to what is necessary for the institution decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims follow independent claim showing at institution
rubrics_metrics.description: When dependent claims depend directly or indirectly from an independent claim that the petitioner shows is unpatentable for institution purposes, the dependent claims that are materially similar will also be treated as sufficiently supported for institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful preliminary showing on an independent claim often supports institution on dependent claims; petitioners should briefly explain how each dependent limitation is taught or suggested by the cited art or the combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary denial under 35 U.S.C. §325(d) — two‑part framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board applies a two‑part framework to decide whether to deny institution under §325(d): (1) whether the same or substantially the same art (or arguments) was previously presented to the Office; and (2) if so, whether the petitioner has demonstrated that the Office erred in a manner material to the patentability of the challenged claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the petition presents previously considered art/arguments, the petitioner must show that the Office committed a material error in its prior consideration to avoid discretionary denial. Evaluate prior Office decisions and whether the petition raises materially different questions or demonstrates prior error.
